subject: biology
title: Practical molecular biology for reading papers
description: Undergraduate/practitioner-level molecular biology for an ML researcher: genes, proteins, pathways, naming, databases, data formats, and ML-for-biology papers. Every lesson defines its terms; no biology beyond high school assumed.
changes: v2: every lesson opens with a Key terms glossary (also exported as the structured `glossary` array) and defines terms where they are first used
v2: every card has an `accept` array for typed-answer checking; multi-part cards rewritten so the typed part is short
v2: new basic-term cards appended to each unit (existing card ids unchanged)

v3: every card audited for typed answers: one unambiguous short answer (≤ ~4 words), the expected form stated in parentheses at the end of the prompt, comparisons/lists split into separate cards (original id kept for the first part, new ids appended)
v3: glossary rewritten to one term per entry; each definition points to exactly one term and never contains it; glossary entries now carry an `accept` array for the Terms drill

v4: 33 figures added to the lessons (32 SVG diagrams drawn for this site plus one public-domain NHGRI karyotype photo) in figures/; each lesson embeds them as a Markdown image line (`![alt](content/biology/figures/<file>)`) followed directly by a `**Figure U.N.** caption` line in the same paragraph. Requires the figure-aware js/markdown.js. Card, quiz and glossary content and ids unchanged; lesson_words now includes caption text

units.title: Central dogma for practitioners
units.summary: How genes are laid out in the genome, how they become transcripts and proteins, and which vocabulary (exons, UTRs, isoforms, reading frames, PTMs) shows up constantly in papers and data. This is the vocabulary everything else builds on.

units.title: Naming conventions and identifiers
units.summary: How to read gene and protein names across species, HLA alleles, HGVS variant notation and rsIDs, and the identifier formats from Ensembl, RefSeq, UniProt, PDB and others. Parsing these on sight is what lets you join datasets and read methods sections.

units.title: Databases and where to find things
units.summary: A map from biological questions to the canonical database that answers them: genes, proteins and structures, expression, variants and disease, pathways and interactions, and raw data archives. Includes the accession formats you'll see in data-availability statements.

units.title: Proteins: sequence, structure, families
units.summary: Amino acid one-letter codes by chemistry, levels of protein structure, domains and the databases that catalog them, AlphaFold confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, ipTM), MSAs and coevolution, and the protein families you'll meet most often in papers.

units.title: Key pathways and signaling
units.summary: The canonical signaling circuits that show up constantly in biology and cancer papers: RTK-RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, p53 and DNA damage, Wnt, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, apoptosis, and the cell cycle, plus the main oncogenes and tumor suppressors and the drugs that target them.

units.title: Data formats and experiments
units.summary: The file formats (FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM/CRAM, VCF, BED, GTF/GFF, h5ad) and coordinate conventions you'll handle, the reference genome builds, and how the main assays work: bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, CRISPR screens, and mass-spec proteomics.

units.title: Reading ML-for-biology papers
units.summary: How to decode the tasks, benchmarks (CASP, ProteinGym/DMS, ClinVar), tokenization choices for proteins, DNA and single cells, leakage-aware data splits, and evaluation metrics in ML-for-biology papers, plus a checklist for reading one quickly.
